Tromino as a Rep-tile

InductionCountingArea
What it shows: One square is missing from a square board, and L-shaped pieces of three squares can fill every other square.
How to play: Click a square to move the gap, then press One step to break the biggest Ls into four smaller ones. Pick a larger board to watch the same picture repeat.

Look for the math

A square board of size 2n × 2n has one square taken away. However big the board and wherever the gap, the rest can be covered exactly by L-trominoes — three unit squares in an L. This applet shows Solomon Golomb's proof by cutting the board into four and repeating the trick.

Cut the board into four

Draw the two middle lines. The gap lies in exactly one of the four equal quarters. Put one L around the middle so that it covers one square in each of the other three quarters. Now all four quarters have a gap: the real one in its own quarter, and the square taken by the middle L in the other three. Each quarter is a smaller copy of the same problem.

An L is four smaller Ls

An L of side s (three squares of side s) can be built from four Ls of side s/2. Their areas match: 4 × 3 × (s/2)² = 3s². The applet places them exactly; the logic test splits every L of side 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 in all four orientations and checks that the four children cover the parent with no overlap and no gap. A shape made of smaller copies of itself like this is a rep-tile.

Why it never fails

Start with the gap in one quarter: the middle L fills the other three, and the quarter with the gap is the same puzzle at half the size. Repeat. This is mathematical induction. The process stops at a 2 × 2 board, where one square gone leaves exactly one L-tromino. So every size works, for every position of the gap. The applet's opening picture already uses that: one L at each size, nested around the gap. Each press of One step replaces every L bigger than the new size by its four copies; on a board of 2e × 2e, a further 2e − 1 presses turn every piece into a single L.

How many pieces?

A 2n × 2n board has 4n squares. One is missing, so there are 4n − 1 left, and each L uses 3. The finished picture therefore has (4n − 1) / 3 pieces. The logic test checks every gap on boards up to 16 × 16, step by step: the pieces never overlap, the gap is never covered, every other square is covered once, and the final count always matches. For the default 16 × 16 board that is (256 − 1) / 3 = 85 pieces after three presses.

Compare a 4 × 4 board with an 8 × 8 one: the first press always splits the biggest L, and the rest of the picture is the old picture with smaller copies inside it. On the 2 × 2 board there is nothing to split, so the first press begins again — that is what the original applet does too.
